Reading · one day, one city, one local

1.1 Discuss with a partner.

1 A friend visits your city for one day. Where do you take them first?

2 Do you prefer famous sights or ordinary streets when you travel?

3 What is the one thing a visitor should not miss?

KEY WORDS

a highlight the best part

a local a person who lives there

skip decide not to do something

worth it good enough to justify the effort

ONE DAY, ONE CITY, ONE LOCAL

We asked a woman who has lived in Istanbul all her life to plan one day for a first-time visitor. Here is what she said.

Start early, and skip the palace. Everyone goes to the palace first. It's magnificent, but by ten o'clock it's so crowded you can't see anything. Go at eight to the fish market instead — it's noisy, it's ugly, and it's the most alive place in the city. Then have breakfast at one of the tiny cafés behind it. You won't find them in any guidebook.

Walk, don't ride. The old streets are narrow and the modern ones are wide and full of traffic, so the old ones are faster on foot. Take the road up the hill behind the mosque — it's steep, and at the top there's an ordinary tea garden with an extraordinary view. Sit there for an hour. Nobody will hurry you.

In the afternoon, go indoors. The heat comes at two. That's the time for the covered market — it's ancient, it's huge, and it's cool. Don't try to see all of it; you'll get lost, and that's fine. When you find a door, go out of it, and you'll be somewhere new.

The evening is the point. Take the ferry across the water at seven. It costs almost nothing and the light is the best in the city. On the other side there's a peaceful street of small restaurants. Eat there, take the last ferry back, and you'll understand why nobody who lives here ever wants to leave.

2

Grammar · will, won't and shall

PRESENTATION

In 4A you learned two futures for things already decided. Will is for the third case — deciding NOW, as you speak.

DECIDE A decision made at the moment of speaking. Would you like tea or coffee? — Er… I'll have tea, please. · So we won't go to the palace, then. The decision did not exist one second earlier.

OFFER An offer. Oh no — I've left my money at home! — Don't worry, I'll pay. · Shall I get the bill? With I, shall is a question that offers.

PROMISE A promise. I promise I won't tell anyone. · You won't miss your flight — I'll drive you.

SUGGEST A suggestion — shall we. Shall we start with something to eat? · What shall we do this evening? The usual reply is Let's + verb: Let's go to the market.

Form. will and shall are modals: one form for every person, no -s, no to. Short forms: 'll and won't. Question: Will you help me? — Yes, I will. / No, I won't. Shall is used almost only in questions with I and we.

Use

Example

decision now

OK — I'll take the blue one.

offer

I'll carry that for you. · Shall I open the window?

promise

I won't be late, I promise.

suggestion

Shall we go to the cinema? — Yes, let's.

request

Will you take a photo of us?

ERROR WARNING

1 Will is not for arrangements. ✗ I will meet Ali on Friday, we arranged it. → ✓ I'm meeting Ali on Friday. If it was decided before now, it is not will.

2 No to after will. ✗ I'll to help you. → ✓ I'll help you.

3 Shall is a question word, not a statement. ✗ We shall go to the market. (possible but very formal and old-fashioned) → ✓ Shall we go to the market? · ✓ Let's go to the market.

4 Answer Shall we…? with Let's, not Yes, we shall. Shall we eat? — ✓ Yes, let's. / ✓ Good idea.

5 Won't is not want. They sound close — won't /wəʊnt/, want /wɒnt/ — and they mean opposite things. I won't go = I refuse. I want to go = I'd like to. Section 3 practises the sounds.

3

Vocabulary · adjectives for places

PRESENTATION

Learn these in opposite pairs — each one is worth two words.

modern ↔ ancient · high ↔ low · indoor ↔ outdoor · magnificent ↔ ordinary

narrow ↔ wide · noisy ↔ peaceful · crowded ↔ empty · huge ↔ tiny · pretty ↔ ugly

Two are not quite symmetrical. Ancient is thousands of years old — a Roman wall, not your grandmother's house; for that, say old. And magnificent is a strong word: it means so impressive you stop and look. Use it for a palace, not a nice café.

And note the strong ones. Huge, tiny, magnificent and ancient are already extreme, so they take absolutely or really, not very: absolutely huge, never ✗ very huge.

PRONUNCIATION — WANT TO /WⱰNT/ AND WON'T /WƏƱNT/

These two are one vowel apart and mean opposite things. want has the short /ɒ/ of hot and not. won't has the long moving /əʊ/ of no and go.

In fast speech want to often becomes /wɒnə/. So the pair to hear is /wɒnə/ versus /wəʊnt/ — a short flat sound against a long sliding one.

Test yourself: I want to see the market. / I won't see the market. Say both slowly. If they sound the same, make the won't longer and rounder — think oh.

WHY YOU DIDN'T HEAR IT

Decisions made while speaking come with a hesitation in front of them. Er… I'll have the noodles. Hmm… so we won't go to the palace. The er and hmm are your signal that a will is coming — the speaker is thinking, then deciding.

And shall we is almost always /ʃəl wi/ or /ʃwi/. It is one quick sound before the verb. If a sentence starts with a verb and ends with a rising voice, there was probably a shall we you didn't catch.

5

Writing · inviting and replying by email

Lesson 4D — Are you free on Saturday? In 4C you invited people out loud. This is the written version — same job, different tools.

AN INVITATION EMAIL HAS FOUR MOVES — IN THIS ORDER

1 Ask how they are. How are you? · How are things? · Hope you're well and enjoying the new job.

2 Ask if they're free. Are you free on Saturday? · Are you doing anything on Saturday evening?

3 Invite. Would you like to come? · Can you come? · We're having a barbecue and inviting a few people.

4 Say you want to see them. It would be lovely to see you and have a chance to chat. · It'd be great to see you!

Notice the tone changes with the friend. To someone you haven't seen for ages: full sentences, It would be lovely. To someone you see every week: How are things?, Can you come?, Love. Same four moves, different register.

REPLYING — THANK, THEN YES OR NO

Thank: Thanks for inviting me. · Thanks for asking. · Nice to hear from you.

Yes: I'd love to come. · I'm free that evening. · Is it OK if I bring…? · I'm looking forward to seeing you and catching up.

No: I'm really sorry, but I'm afraid I can't come. · I'd love to, but… · Thanks for asking. Maybe next time?

A no has three parts — sorry, can't, reason (optional). I'm afraid softens it; I'd love to, but shows you wanted to. Leave out both and the same words sound cold.

5.1 Read the two invitations. Answer the questions.

TWO EMAILS FROM NILUFAR

To Kamola: Hi Kamola, How are you? We haven't seen you for ages! Hope you're well and the new flat is working out. We're having a picnic by the lake on Sunday. Are you free, and if so, would you like to come? People are arriving around one. Everyone's bringing something — could you bring some fruit? It would be lovely to see you and have a proper catch-up. Best wishes, Nilufar

To Bek: Hi Bek, How are things? Hope the football went well on Saturday! Are you doing anything on Sunday? We're having a picnic by the lake — can you come? Everyone's bringing something. We'll do the drinks, but could you bring some bread? It'd be great to see you! Love, Nilufar

She's staying with me that weekend. We'll bring fruit and something sweet. Looking forward to seeing you and catching up properly.

5.3 Correct the mistake in each sentence. These are the four errors everyone makes.

1 You like to come to my birthday party?

2 Thanks that you invited me to your wedding.

3 It's afraid I can't go to the cinema with you.

4 I love to come, but I'm busy that weekend.

WHY THOSE FOUR

1 An invitation needs Would you like…? — a question without would is not an invitation, it's a survey. 2 Thanks for + -ing, always. 3 I'm afraid is a person being sorry, not a fact being afraid. 4 I'd love to — the 'd is the whole meaning: I would, if I could. Without it you are announcing that you love coming.

If no: I'm afraid + I'd love to, but.
